newsitem.title: INDIA: Murdoch's STAR pushes for India pay channel launch.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch's STAR pushes for India pay channel launch.

text.p: Media baron Rupert Murdoch's loss-making STAR TV is fighting in court and negotiating with the Indian government to revoke a ban on direct-to-home (DTH) satellite broadcasting to protect a $300-million investment.

A senior executive of News Television India, a subsidiary of the News Corp Ltd-owned STAR, told Reuters on Thursday that the company was ready to accept any government conditions to carry forward its plans to launch India's first DTH service.

"We have offered in writing to the Information and Broadcasting Ministry that we are willing to accept any sort of conditionalities it wants to impose if, in the meanwhile, we are allowed to start the service," Urmila Gupta said.
"We have already incurred expenditure of more than $300 million in launching our DTH service," said Gupta, News Television's executive director.
Last week, India banned DTH services, saying they could not be launched until the government passed a law to break a state monopoly over the airwaves.

News Television on Monday challenged the government's ban on DTH in the Delhi High Court, saying the government had the right to regulate electronic media but not prohibit it. The court has asked government agencies to respond to the plea.

The government's Broadcast Bill, expected to be moved in parliament for approval later this year, aims to usher in private broadcasters, who currently can only rent time-slots on state television and radio, not own broadcast stations.
A tentative draft of the bill is being considered by a committee of lawmakers who will suggest changes.
In the current form, STAR would have to bid in an auction for a licence to start DTH services, plans for which were started by STAR months before the bill was proposed.

STAR already has a popular free-to-air service in India on the C-band that requires large antennae used mainly by cable television operators. The DTH service would use smaller KU-band antennae directed at homes.

"We are trying to explain to the authorities that DTH is not very different from what already exists," Gupta told Reuters. She said direct-to-home services already existed in some 900,000 Indian homes, but without using KU-band equipment.
"If we are not included in the bidding when it takes place, we are willing to shut shop and go home," Gupta said.
Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy said on Wednesday that the ban was a temporary measure until the new law came into being.
"DTH will be duly instituted through a bidding process," Reddy said, adding: "I am not like King Canute asking the technological waves to stop."

Gupta said STAR had indefinitely postponed the launch date of its DTH service. "What they're really saying is, don't do anything for the next year or year and a half while we examine the new law," she said.
